title: Γαλῆ καὶ Ἀφροδίτη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 76 (= Perry 50). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γαλῆ ἐρασθεῖσα νεανίσκου εὐπρέπους ηὔξατο τῇ Ἀφροδίτῃ ὅπως αὐτὴν μεταμορφώσῃ εἰς γυναῖκα.
sentences.tr: Galē erastheisa neaniskou euprepous ēuxato tēi Aphroditēi hopōs autēn metamorphōsēi eis gynaika.
sentences.l: A weasel, having fallen in love with a comely young man, prayed to Aphrodite that she might change her into a woman.
sentences.n: The γαλῆ is the house weasel or marten, kept in Greek homes to kill mice — the domestic animal where a modern reader expects a cat. ἐράω takes the genitive of the person loved (νεανίσκου). ὅπως with the subjunctive after a verb of praying is the object clause of effort: 'that she should…'. Aphrodite is the natural god to ask, since the request is made out of desire.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ θεὸς ἐλεήσασα αὐτῆς τὸ πάθος μετετύπωσεν αὐτὴν εἰς κόρην εὐειδῆ, καὶ οὕτως ὁ νεανίσκος θεασάμενος αὐτὴν καὶ ἐρασθεὶς οἴκαδε ὡς ἑαυτὸν ἀπήγαγε.
sentences.tr: Kai hē theos eleēsasa autēs to pathos metetypōsen autēn eis korēn eueidē, kai houtōs ho neaniskos theasamenos autēn kai erastheis oikade hōs heauton apēgage.
sentences.l: And the goddess, having pitied her passion, recast her into a fair-formed maiden, and thus the young man, having seen her and having fallen in love, led her away home to his own house.
sentences.i: The goddess took pity on her longing and remade her as a lovely girl; and so the young man saw her, fell in love, and took her home to his own house.
sentences.n: ἡ θεός: Greek uses the one noun θεός for god and goddess alike, and marks the sex with the article. μετετύπωσεν is from τύπος, a stamp or mould — she was struck into a new shape, not merely altered. οἴκαδε ὡς ἑαυτόν doubles the destination, 'homeward, to his own place'.

sentences.t: Καθημένων δὲ αὐτῶν ἐν τῷ θαλάμῳ, ἡ Ἀφροδίτη γνῶναι βουλομένη εἰ μεταβαλοῦσα τὸ σῶμα ἡ γαλῆ καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἤλλαξε, μῦν εἰς τὸ μέσον καθῆκεν.
sentences.tr: Kathēmenōn de autōn en tōi thalamōi, hē Aphroditē gnōnai boulomenē ei metabalousa to sōma hē galē kai ton tropon ēllaxe, myn eis to meson kathēken.
sentences.l: And they sitting in the bedchamber, Aphrodite, wishing to know whether the weasel, having changed her body, had changed her character also, let a mouse down into the middle.
sentences.i: As the two of them sat in the bridal chamber, Aphrodite, wanting to know whether the weasel had changed her ways along with her body, let a mouse loose in the middle of the room.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (καθημένων αὐτῶν) sets the scene. εἰ after a verb of knowing is 'whether', introducing an indirect question. The test turns on the pairing μεταβαλοῦσα τὸ σῶμα / τὸν τρόπον ἤλλαξε — two verbs for changing, one for the body, one for the character; the fable's whole question is whether the second follows the first.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἐπιλαθομένη τῶν παρόντων ἐξαναστᾶσα ἀπὸ τῆς κοίτης τὸν μῦν ἐδίωκε καταφαγεῖν θέλουσα.
sentences.tr: Hē de epilathomenē tōn parontōn exanastasa apo tēs koitēs ton myn ediōke kataphagein thelousa.
sentences.l: But she, having forgotten the things present, having sprung up from the bed, chased the mouse, wishing to devour it.
sentences.i: But she forgot where she was, sprang up from the bed and ran after the mouse, meaning to eat it.
sentences.n: ἐπιλανθάνομαι takes the genitive of what is forgotten; τῶν παρόντων, 'the things at hand', is her whole present situation — bridegroom, chamber and human shape at once.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ θεὸς ἀγανακτήσασα κατ’ αὐτῆς πάλιν αὐτὴν εἰς τὴν ἀρχαίαν φύσιν ἀποκατέστησεν.
sentences.tr: Kai hē theos aganaktēsasa kat' autēs palin autēn eis tēn archaian physin apokatestēsen.
sentences.l: And the goddess, having grown indignant at her, restored her again to her ancient nature.
sentences.n: ἀγανακτέω κατά with the genitive, 'to be angry against'. ἀποκατέστησεν is a doubly-prefixed compound (ἀπό + κατά + ἵστημι): set her back down again where she was.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ φύσει πονηροί, κἂν φύσιν ἀλλάξωσι, τὸν γοῦν τρόπον οὐ μεταβάλλονται.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi physei ponēroi, kan physin allaxōsi, ton goun tropon ou metaballontai.
sentences.l: So too those among men who are wicked by nature, even if they change their nature, their character at any rate they do not change.
sentences.n: κἄν is καὶ ἐάν by crasis, with the subjunctive ἀλλάξωσι: 'even if they should change'. φύσει is a dative of respect, 'in respect of nature'. γοῦν concedes and narrows at once — 'their character, at any rate, whatever else may alter'.
